entries.7dedab3cb944f12a117c7aee98ca6996c58a55e2: <div sID="gen12319" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="103" osisID="Ps.103" sID="Ps.103"/> <div eID="gen12319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12320" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12321" type="x-p"/> This psalm calls more for devotion than exposition; it is a most excellent psalm of praise, and of general use. The psalmist, I. Stirs up himself and his own soul to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.1-Ps.102.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) for his favour to him in particular (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.3-Ps.102.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), to the church in general, and to all good men, to whom he is, and will be, just, and kind, and constant (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.6-Ps.102.18">ver. 6-18</reference>), and for his government of the world, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.19">ver. 19</reference>. II. He desires the assistance of the holy angels, and all the works of God, in praising him, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.20-Ps.102.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. In singing this psalm we must in a special manner get our hearts affected with the goodness of God and enlarged in love and thankfulness.
entries.44defb97bd581617fe48cf93c9ba0a9b03bb64ed: <div eID="gen12321" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12320" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cheerful Praise.</title> <div sID="gen12322" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul: and all that is within me, <hi type="italic">bless</hi> his holy name. 2 Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul, and forget not all his benefits: <hi type="super">3</hi> Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases; <hi type="super">4</hi> Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies; <hi type="super">5</hi> Who satisfieth thy mouth with good <hi type="italic">things; so that</hi> thy youth is renewed like the eagle's. <div eID="gen12322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12323" type="x-p"/> David is here communing with his own heart, and he is no fool that thus talks to himself and excites his own soul to that which is good. Observe, <div eID="gen12323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12324" type="x-p"/> I. How he stirs up himself to the duty of praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1-Ps.103.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. 1. It is the Lord that is to be blessed and spoken well of; for he is the fountain of all good, whatever are the channels or cisterns; it is to his name, his holy name, that we are to consecrate our praise, <hi type="italic">giving thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.</hi> 2. It is the soul that is to be employed in blessing God, <hi type="italic">and all that is within</hi> us. We make nothing of our religious performances if we do not make heart-work of them, if that which is within us, nay, if <hi type="italic">all that is within</hi> us, be not engaged in them. The work requires the inward man, the whole man, and all little enough. 3. In order to our return of praises to God, there must be a grateful remembrance of the mercies we have received from him: <hi type="italic">Forget not all his benefits.</hi> If we do not give thanks for them, we do forget them; and that is unjust as well as unkind, since in all God's favours there is so much that is memorable. "O my soul! to thy shame be it spoken, thou hast forgotten many of his benefits; but surely thou wilt not forget them all, for thou shouldst not have forgotten any." <div eID="gen12324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12325" type="x-p"/> II. How he furnishes himself with abundant matter for praise, and that which is very affecting: "Come, my soul, consider what God has done for thee." 1. "He has pardoned thy sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">v. 3</reference>); he has forgiven, and <hi type="italic">does forgive, all thy iniquities.</hi>" This is mentioned first because by the pardon of sin that is taken away which kept good things from us, and we are restored to the favour of God, which bestows good things on us. Think what the provocation was; it was iniquity, and yet pardoned; how many the provocations were, and yet all pardoned. <hi type="italic">He has forgiven all our trespasses.</hi> It is a continued act; he is still forgiving, as we are still sinning and repenting. 2. "He has cured thy sickness." The corruption of nature is the sickness of the soul; it is its disorder, and threatens its death. This is cured in sanctification; when sin is mortified, the disease is healed; though complicated, it is all healed. Our crimes were capital, but God saves our lives by pardoning them; our diseases were mortal, but God saves our lives by healing them. These two go together; for, as for God, his work is perfect and not done by halves; if God take away the guilt of sin by pardoning mercy, he will break the power of it by renewing grace. Where Christ is made righteousness to any soul he is made sanctification, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1 Cor. i. 30</reference>. 3. "He has rescued thee from danger." A man may be in peril of life, not only by his crimes, or his diseases, but by the power of his enemies; and therefore here also we experience the divine goodness: <hi type="italic">Who redeemed thy life from destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.4">v. 4</reference>), from the destroyer, <hi type="italic">from hell</hi> (so the Chaldee), from the second death. <hi type="italic">The redemption of the soul is precious;</hi> we cannot compass it, and therefore are the more indebted to divine grace that has wrought it out, to him who has <hi type="italic">obtained eternal redemption for us.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Job.33.24">Job xxxiii. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">28</reference>. 4. "He has not only saved thee from death and ruin, but has made thee truly and completely happy, with honour, pleasure, and long life." (1.) "He has given thee true honour and great honour, no less than a crown: <hi type="italic">He crowns thee with his lovingkindness and tender mercies;</hi>" and what greater dignity is a poor soul capable of than to be advanced into the love and favour of God? <hi type="italic">This honour have all his saints.</hi> What is the crown of glory but God's favour? (2.) "He has given thee true pleasure: <hi type="italic">He satisfies thy mouth with good things</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">v. 5</reference>); it is only the favour and grace of God that can give satisfaction to a soul, can suit its capacities, supply its needs, and answer to its desires. Nothing but divine wisdom can undertake to <hi type="italic">fill its treasures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>); other things will surfeit, but not <hi type="italic">satiate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Eccl. vi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. (3.) "He has given thee a prospect and pledge of long life: <hi type="italic">Thy youth is renewed like the eagle's.</hi>" The eagle is long-lived, and, as naturalists say, when she is nearly 100 years old, casts all her feathers (as indeed she changes them in a great measure every year at moulting time), and fresh ones come, so that she becomes young again. When God, by the graces and comforts of his Spirit, recovers his people from their decays, and fills them with new life and joy, which is to them an earnest of eternal life and joy, then they may be said to <hi type="italic">return to the days of their youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job xxxiii. 25</reference>.
entries.a5675e249aaf85d1dd612b4ebde0518344a1952b: <div eID="gen12325" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Goodness and Compassion of God.</title> <div sID="gen12326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed. 7 He made known his ways unto Moses, his acts unto the children of Israel. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. <hi type="super">9</hi> He will not always chide: neither will he keep <hi type="italic">his anger</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">10</hi> He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. <hi type="super">11</hi> For as the heaven is high above the earth, <hi type="italic">so</hi> great is his mercy toward them that fear him. <hi type="super">12</hi> As far as the east is from the west, <hi type="italic">so</hi> far hath he removed our transgressions from us. <hi type="super">13</hi> Like as a father pitieth <hi type="italic">his</hi> children, <hi type="italic">so</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> pitieth them that fear him. <hi type="super">14</hi> For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we <hi type="italic">are</hi> dust. 15 <hi type="italic">As for</hi> man, his days <hi type="italic">are</hi> as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. <hi type="super">16</hi> For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more. <hi type="super">17</hi> But the mercy of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children's children; <hi type="super">18</hi> To such as keep his covenant, and to those that remember his commandments to do them. <div eID="gen12326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12327" type="x-p"/> Hitherto the psalmist had only looked back upon his own experiences and thence fetched matter for praise; here he looks abroad and takes notice of his favour to others also; for in them we should rejoice and give thanks for them, all the saints being fed at a common table and sharing in the same blessings. <div eID="gen12327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12328" type="x-p"/> I. Truly God is good to all (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">v. 6</reference>): He <hi type="italic">executes righteousness and judgment,</hi> not only for his own people, but <hi type="italic">for all that are oppressed;</hi> for even in common providence he is the patron of wronged innocency, and, one way or other, will plead the cause of those that are injured against their oppressors. It is his honour to humble the proud and help the helpless. <div eID="gen12328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12329" type="x-p"/> II. He is in a special manner good to Israel, to every Israelite indeed, that is of a clean and upright heart. <div eID="gen12329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12330" type="x-p"/> 1. He has revealed himself and his grace to us (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He made known his ways unto Moses,</hi> and by him <hi type="italic">his acts to the children of Israel,</hi> not only by his rod to those who then lived, but by his pen to succeeding ages. Note, Divine revelation is one of the first and greatest of divine favours with which the church is blessed; for God restores us to himself by revealing himself to us, and gives us all good by giving us knowledge. He has <hi type="italic">made known his acts and his ways</hi> (that is, his nature, and the methods of his dealing with the children of men), that they may know both what to conceive of him and what to expect from him; so Dr. Hammond. Or by his <hi type="italic">ways</hi> we may understand his precepts, the way which he requires us to walk in; and by his <hi type="italic">acts,</hi> or <hi type="italic">designs</hi> (as the word signifies), his promises and purposes as to what he will do with us. Thus fairly does God deal with us. <div eID="gen12330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12331" type="x-p"/> 2. He has never been rigorous and severe with us, but always tender, full of compassion, and ready to forgive. <div eID="gen12331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12332" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is in his nature to be so (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is merciful and gracious;</hi> this was his way which he made known unto Moses at Mount Horeb, when he thus proclaimed his name (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7">Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7</reference>), in answer to Moses's request (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.13">ch. xxxiii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">I beseech thee, show me thy way, that I may know thee.</hi> It is my way, says God, to pardon sin. [1.] He is not soon angry, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.8">v. 8</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">slow to anger,</hi> not extreme to mark what we do amiss nor ready to take advantage against us. He bears long with those that are very provoking, defers punishing, that he may give space to repent, and does not speedily execute the sentence of his law; and he could not be thus <hi type="italic">slow to anger</hi> if he were not <hi type="italic">plenteous in mercy,</hi> the very <hi type="italic">Father of mercies.</hi> [2.] He is not long angry; for (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">v. 9</reference>) <hi type="italic">he will not always chide,</hi> though we always offend and deserve chiding. Though he signify his displeasure against us for our sins by the rebukes of Providence, and the reproaches of our own consciences, and thus cause grief, yet he will have compassion, and will not always keep us in pain and terror, no, not for our sins, but, after the spirit of bondage, will give the spirit of adoption. How unlike are those to God who always chide, who take every occasion to chide, and never know when to cease! What would become of us if God should deal so with us? <hi type="italic">He will not keep his anger for ever</hi> against his own people, but will gather them with <hi type="italic">everlasting mercies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">Isa. liv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.16">lvii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen12332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12333" type="x-p"/> (2.) We have found him so; we, for our parts, must own that <hi type="italic">he has not dealt with us after our sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.10">v. 10</reference>. The scripture says a great deal of the mercy of God, and we may all set to our seal that it is true, that we have experienced it. If he had not been a God of patience, we should have been in hell long ago; but <hi type="italic">he has not rewarded us after our iniquities;</hi> so those will say who know what sin deserves. He has not inflicted the judgments which we have merited, nor deprived us of the comforts which we have forfeited, which should make us think the worse, and not the better, of sin; for <hi type="italic">God's patience should lead us to repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Rom. ii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen12333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12334" type="x-p"/> 3. He has pardoned our sins, not only my <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">v. 3</reference>), but <hi type="italic">our transgressions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.12">v. 12</reference>. Though it is of our own benefit, by the pardoning mercy of God, that we are to take the comfort, yet of the benefit others have by it we must give him the glory. Observe, (1.) The transcendent riches of God's mercy (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the heaven is high above the earth</hi> (so high that the earth is but a point to the vast expanse), so God's mercy is above the merits of those that fear him most, so much above and beyond them that there is no proportion at all between them; the greatest performances of man's duty cannot demand the least tokens of God's favour as a debt, and therefore all the seed of Jacob will join with him in owning themselves <hi type="italic">less than the least of all God's mercies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.32.10">Gen. xxxii. 10</reference>. Observe, God's mercy is thus great <hi type="italic">towards those that fear him,</hi> not towards those that trifle with him. We must fear the Lord and his goodness. (2.) The fulness of his pardons, an evidence of the riches of his mercy (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">As far as the east is from the west</hi> (which two quarters of the world are of greatest extent, because all known and inhabited, and therefore geographers that way reckon their longitudes) <hi type="italic">so far has he removed our transgressions from us,</hi> so that they shall never be laid to our charge, nor rise up in judgment against us. The sins of believers shall be remembered no more, shall not be mentioned unto them; they shall be sought for, and not found. If we thoroughly forsake them, God will thoroughly forgive them. <div eID="gen12334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12335" type="x-p"/> 4. He has pitied our sorrows, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.13-Ps.103.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Observe, (1.) Whom he pities—<hi type="italic">those that fear him,</hi> that is, all good people, who in this world may become objects of pity on account of the grievances to which they are not only born, but born again. Or it may be understood of those who have not yet received <hi type="italic">the spirit of adoption,</hi> but are yet <hi type="italic">trembling at his word;</hi> those he <hi type="italic">pities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jer. xxxi. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">20</reference>. (2.) How he pities—<hi type="italic">as a father pities his children,</hi> and does them good as there is occasion. God is a Father to those that fear him and owns them for his children, and he is tender of them as a father. The father pities his children that are weak in knowledge and instructs them, pities them when they are froward and bears with them, pities them when they are sick and comforts them (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.13">Isa. lxvi. 13</reference>), pities them when they have fallen and helps them up again, pities them when they have offended, and, upon their submission, forgives them, pities them when they are wronged and gives them redress; thus <hi type="italic">the Lord pities those that fear him.</hi> (3.) Why he pities—<hi type="italic">for he knows our frame.</hi> He has reason to know our frame, for he framed us; and, having himself made man of the dust, <hi type="italic">he remembers that he is dust,</hi> not only by constitution, but by sentence. <hi type="italic">Dust thou art.</hi> He considers the frailty of our bodies and the folly of our souls, how little we can do, and expects accordingly from us, how little we can bear, and lays accordingly upon us, in all which appears the tenderness of his compassion. <div eID="gen12335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12336" type="x-p"/> 5. He has perpetuated his covenant-mercy and thereby provided relief for our frailty, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.15-Ps.103.18">v. 15-18</reference>. See here, (1.) How short man's life is and of what uncertain continuance. The lives even of great men and good men are so, and neither their greatness nor their goodness can alter the property of them: <hi type="italic">As for man, his days are as grass,</hi> which grows out of the earth, rises but a little way above it, and soon withers and returns to it again. See <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.7">Isa. xl. 6, 7</reference>. Man, in his best estate, seems somewhat more than grass; he flourishes and looks gay; yet then he is but <hi type="italic">like a flower of the field,</hi> which, though distinguished a little from the grass, will wither with it. The flower of the garden is commonly more choice and valuable, and, though in its own nature withering, will last the longer for its being sheltered by the garden wall and the gardener's care; but the flower of the field (to which life is here compared) is not only withering in itself, but exposed to the cold blasts, and liable to be cropped and trodden on by the beasts of the field. Man's life is not only wasting of itself, but its period may be anticipated by a thousand accidents. When the flower is in its perfection a blasting wind, unseen, unlooked for, <hi type="italic">passes over it, and it is gone;</hi> it hangs the head, drops the leaves, dwindles into the ground again, <hi type="italic">and the place thereof,</hi> which was proud of it, now <hi type="italic">knows it no more.</hi> Such a thing is man: God considers this, and pities him; let him consider it himself, and be humble, dead to this world and thoughtful of another. (2.) How long and lasting God's mercy is to his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.17-Ps.103.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): it will continue longer than their lives, and will survive their present state. Observe, [1.] The description of those to whom this mercy belongs. They are such as fear God, such as are truly religious, from principle. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They live a life of faith; for they <hi type="italic">keep God's covenant;</hi> having taken hold of it, they keep hold of it, fast hold, and will not let it go. They keep it as a treasure, keep it as their portion, and would not for all the world part with it, for it is their life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They live a life of obedience; they <hi type="italic">remember his commandments to do them,</hi> else they do not <hi type="italic">keep his covenant.</hi> Those only shall have the benefit of God's promises that make conscience of his precepts. See who those are that have a good memory, as well as a <hi type="italic">good understanding</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Ps. cxi. 10</reference>), those that <hi type="italic">remember God's commandments,</hi> not to talk of them, but <hi type="italic">to do them,</hi> and to be ruled by them. [2.] The continuance of the mercy which belongs to such as these; it will last them longer than their lives on earth, and therefore they need not be troubled though their lives be short, since death itself will be no abridgment, no infringement, of their bliss. God's mercy is better than life, for it will out-live it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To their souls, which are immortal; to them the mercy of the Lord is <hi type="italic">from everlasting to everlasting;</hi> from everlasting in the councils of it to everlasting in the consequences of it, in their election before the world was and their glorification when this world shall be no more; for they are predestinated to the <hi type="italic">inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>) and <hi type="italic">look for the mercy of the Lord,</hi> the Lord Jesus, unto eternal life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To their seed, which shall be kept up to the end of time (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.28">Ps. cii. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">His righteousness,</hi> the truth of his promise, shall be <hi type="italic">unto children's children;</hi> provided they tread in the steps of their predecessors' piety, and <hi type="italic">keep his covenant,</hi> as they did, then shall mercy be preserved to them, even to <hi type="italic">a thousand generations.</hi>
entries.2c9e5f9dd4ade4c93a6daa45339ee123f9bbc37a: <div eID="gen12336" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cheerful Praise.</title> <div sID="gen12337" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all. <hi type="super">20</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word. <hi type="super">21</hi> Bless ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> his hosts; <hi type="italic">ye</hi> ministers of his, that do his pleasure. <hi type="super">22</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all his works in all places of his dominion: bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul. <div eID="gen12337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12338" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The doctrine of universal providence laid down, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">v. 19</reference>. He has secured the happiness of his peculiar people by promise and covenant, but the order of mankind, and the world in general, he secures by common providence. <hi type="italic">The Lord has a throne</hi> of his own, a throne of glory, a throne of government. He that made all rules all, and both by a word of power: <hi type="italic">He has prepared his throne,</hi> has fixed and established it that it cannot be shaken; he has afore-ordained all the measures of his government and does all according to the counsel of his own will. He <hi type="italic">has prepared</hi> it <hi type="italic">in the heavens,</hi> above us, and out of sight; for he <hi type="italic">holds back the face of his throne, and spreads a cloud upon it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job xxvi. 9</reference>); yet he can himself <hi type="italic">judge through the dark cloud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job xxiii. 13</reference>. Hence <hi type="italic">the heavens are said to rule</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.26">Dan. iv. 26</reference>), and we are led to consider this by the influence which even the visible heavens have upon this earth, their <hi type="italic">dominion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.33">Job xxxviii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.1.16">Gen. i. 16</reference>. But though God's throne is in heaven, and there he keeps his court, and thither we are to direct to him (<hi type="italic">Our Father who art in heaven</hi>), yet <hi type="italic">his kingdom rules over all.</hi> He takes cognizance of all the inhabitants, and all the affairs, of this lower world, and disposes all persons and things according to the counsel of his will, to his own glory (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.35">Dan. iv. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">His kingdom rules over all</hi> kings and all kingdoms, and from it there is no exempt jurisdiction. <div eID="gen12338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12339" type="x-p"/> II. The duty of universal praise inferred from it: if all are under God's dominion, all must do him homage. <div eID="gen12339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12340" type="x-p"/> 1. Let the holy angels praise him (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.20-Ps.103.21">v. 20, 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, you his angels;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, all you his hosts, you ministers of his.</hi> David had been stirring up himself and others to praise God, and here, in the close, he calls upon the angels to do it; not as if they needed any excitement of ours to praise God, they do it continually; but thus he expresses his high thoughts of God as worthy of the adorations of the holy angels, thus he quickens himself and others to the duty with this consideration, That it is the work of angels, and comforts himself in reference to his own weakness and defect in the performance of this duty with this consideration, That there is a world of holy angels who dwell in God's house and are still praising him. In short, the blessed angels are glorious attendants upon the blessed God. Observe, (1.) How well qualified they are for the post they are in. They are able; for they <hi type="italic">excel in strength;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">mighty in strength</hi> (so the word is); they are able to bring great things to pass, and to abide in their work without weariness. And they are as willing as they are able; they are willing to know their work; for they <hi type="italic">hearken to the voice of his word;</hi> they stand expecting commission and instructions from their great Lord, and <hi type="italic">always behold his face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.10">Matt. xviii. 10</reference>), that they may take the first intimation of his mind. They are willing to do their work: They <hi type="italic">do his commandments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">v. 20</reference>); they <hi type="italic">do his pleasure</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">v. 21</reference>); they dispute not any divine commands, but readily address themselves to the execution of them. Nor do they delay, but fly swiftly: They <hi type="italic">do his commandments at hearing,</hi> or <hi type="italic">as soon as they hear the voice of his word;</hi> so Dr. Hammond. <hi type="italic">To obey is better than sacrifice;</hi> for angels obey, but do not sacrifice. (2.) What their service is. They are <hi type="italic">his angels,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ministers of his</hi>—his, for he made them, and made them for himself—his, for he employs them, though he does not need them—his, for he is their owner and Lord; they belong to him and he has them at his beck. All the creatures are his servants, but not as the angels that attend the presence of his glory. Soldiers, and seamen, and all good subjects, serve the king, but not as the courtiers do, the ministers of state and those of the household. [1.] The angels occasionally serve God in this lower world; they <hi type="italic">do his commandments,</hi> go on his errands (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan. ix. 21</reference>), fight his battles (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings vi. 17</reference>), and minister for the good of his people, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">Heb. i. 14</reference>. [2.] They <hi type="italic">continually praise him</hi> in the upper world; they began betimes to do it (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 7</reference>), and it is still their business, from which they rest not <hi type="italic">day nor night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>. It is God's glory that he has such attendants, but more his glory that he neither needs them nor is benefited by them. <div eID="gen12340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12341" type="x-p"/> 2. Let <hi type="italic">all his works</hi> praise him (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.22">v. 22</reference>), all <hi type="italic">in all places of his dominion;</hi> for, because they are his works, they are under his dominion, and they were made and are ruled that they may be unto him <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise. All his works,</hi> that is, all the children of men, in all parts of the world, let them all praise God; yea, and the inferior creatures too, which are God's works also; let them praise him objectively, though they cannot praise him actually, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.10">Ps. cxlv. 10</reference>. Yet all this shall not excuse David from praising God, but rather excite him to do it the more cheerfully, that he may bear a part in this concert; for he concludes, <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, O my soul!</hi> as he began, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">v. 1</reference>. Blessing God and giving him glory must be the alpha and the omega of all our services. He began with <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, O my soul!</hi> and, when he had penned and sung this excellent hymn to his honour, he does not say, Now, O my soul! thou hast blessed the Lord, sit down, and rest thee, but, <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, O my soul!</hi> yet more and more. When we have done ever so much in the service of God, yet still we must stir up ourselves to do more. God's praise is a subject that will never be exhausted, and therefore we must never think this work done till we come to heaven, where it will be for ever in the doing.  <chapter eID="Ps.103"/> <div eID="gen12341" type="x-p"/>

entries.7bceca7be78352fba871fc3745b42c77cb744c98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6670"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 103</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.103.1-Ps.103.22">Psa 103:1-22</reference>. A Psalm of joyous praise, in which the writer rises from a thankful acknowledgment of personal blessings to a lively celebration of God's gracious attributes, as not only intrinsically worthy of praise, but as specially suited to man's frailty. He concludes by invoking all creatures to unite in his song.</title> <div sID="gen10213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6670"/><hi type="bold">1. Bless, &c.--</hi>when God is the object, praise.<div eID="gen10213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my soul--</hi>myself (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">25:1</reference>), with allusion to the act, as one of intelligence.<div eID="gen10214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... within me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.6.5">De 6:5</reference>).<div eID="gen10215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his holy name--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>), His complete moral perfections. <div eID="gen10216" type="x-p"/>

entries.76e37949ba5818da6b2d496c65bad5bc99e11e1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6674"/><div sID="gen10223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6674"/>5. By God's provision, the saint retains a youthful vigor like the eagles (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.14">Psa 92:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>). <div eID="gen10223" type="x-p"/>

Literally, "righteousness and judgments," denoting various acts of God's government. <div eID="gen10224" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c531bf87ae16cd114b3b91a5e753c11125a1de4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6676"/><div sID="gen10225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6676"/><hi type="bold">7. ways--</hi>of providence, &c., as usual (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">67:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">acts--</hi>literally, "wonders" (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.11">Psa 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.17">78:17</reference>). <div eID="gen10226" type="x-p"/>

entries.9922de3b844825faeb41c7fbc52bb4a9ead56655: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6681"/><div sID="gen10232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6681"/><hi type="bold">14. he--</hi>"who formed," <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>.<div eID="gen10232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth our frame--</hi>literally, "our form."<div eID="gen10233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we are dust--</hi>made of and tending to it (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10234" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d101cbb08b9b2473f3909a3c941686780858b10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6682"/><div sID="gen10235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6682"/>15-16. So short and frail is life that a breath may destroy it.<div eID="gen10235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is gone--</hi>literally, "it is not."<div eID="gen10236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know it no more--</hi>no more recognize him (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">Psa 90:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Is 40:6-8</reference>). <div eID="gen10237" type="x-p"/>

entries.ead14d39a5443cfbe388022e43ab44dec61cb818: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6685"/><div sID="gen10241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6685"/>19. God's firm and universal dominion is a pledge that He will keep His promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.47.8">47:8</reference>). <div eID="gen10241" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2a164c905119eb9e2623d7f62f8f8edb00ec1fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6686"/><div sID="gen10242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6686"/><hi type="bold">20-22. do his commandments ... word--</hi>or, literally, "so as to hearken," &c., that is, their acts of obedience are prompt, so that they are ever ready to hear, and know, and follow implicitly His declared will (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.26.17">De 26:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.19">Lu 1:19</reference>). <div eID="gen10242" type="x-p"/>

entries.4c00b40311a70c7f9e22d7ab41978810921a0814: <div eID="gen22011" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22012" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22013" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22013" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22012" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22014" type="x-p"/> God is praised for his benefits to his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.1">Psa 103:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.2">Psa 103:2</reference>; he forgives their iniquities, and heals their diseases, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; redeems their lives, crowns them with loving-kindness, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.4">Psa 103:4</reference>; satisfies them with good things, renews their youth, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>; he helps the oppressed, makes his ways known, is merciful and gracious, and keeps not his anger for ever, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.6-Psa.103.9">Psa 103:6-9</reference>; his forbearance, and pardoning mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.10-Psa.103.12">Psa 103:10-12</reference>; he is a tender and considerate Father, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.13">Psa 103:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>; the frail state of man, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.15">Psa 103:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>; God's everlasting mercy, and universal dominion, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.17-Psa.103.19">Psa 103:17-19</reference>; all his angels, his hosts, and his works, are invited to praise him, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.20-Psa.103.22">Psa 103:20-22</reference>. <div eID="gen22014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22015" type="x-p"/> The inscription in the Hebrew, and in all the Versions, gives this Psalm to David; and yet many of the ancients believed it to refer to the times of the captivity, or rather to its conclusion, in which the redeemed Jews give thanks to God for their restoration. It is a Psalm of inimitable sweetness and excellence; contains the most affectionate sentiments of gratitude to God for his mercies; and the most consoling motives to continue to trust in God, and be obedient to him. <div eID="gen22015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22016" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22017" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord - He calls on his soul, and all its faculties and powers, to magnify God for his mercies. Under such a weight of obligation the lips can do little; the soul and all its powers must be engaged.
entries.4727c006e03126de226fd9f363dab22add3656d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22018" type="x-p"/> Forget not all his benefits - Call them into recollection; particularize the chief of them; and here record them for an everlasting memorial.
entries.ceef00b724243c248b01935cf384cc8a924eb3b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22019" type="x-p"/> Who forgiveth - The benefits are the following, <div eID="gen22019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22020" type="x-p"/> 1. Forgiveness of sin. <div eID="gen22020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22021" type="x-p"/> 2. Restoration of health: "Who healeth all thy diseases."
entries.1e658ba139fa5eee8f2d282037189f2eea2a4ea0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22022" type="x-p"/> Who redeemeth - <div eID="gen22022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22023" type="x-p"/> 3. Preservation from destruction. הגואל haggoel, properly, redemption of life by the kinsman; possibly looking forward, in the spirit of prophecy, to him who became partaker of our flesh and blood, that he might have the right to redeem our souls from death by dying in our stead. <div eID="gen22023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22024" type="x-p"/> 4. Changing and ennobling his state; weaving a crown for him out of loving-kindness and tender mercies.
entries.044132e15652994e18652c5eac48c426e94c5418: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22025" type="x-p"/> Who satisfieth thy mouth - <div eID="gen22025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22026" type="x-p"/> 5. For continual communications of spiritual and temporal good; so that the vigor of his mind was constantly supported and increased. <div eID="gen22026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22027" type="x-p"/> Thy youth is renewed like the eagle's - There is such a vast variety of the eagle, or genus Falco, that it is not easy to determine which is meant here. <div eID="gen22027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22028" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew נשר neser is a general name for such as were known in the land of Judea; which were probably such as belong to the genus Aquila, comprehending forty-one species and seven varieties. <div eID="gen22028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22029" type="x-p"/> There are as many legends of the eagle among the ancient writers, as there are of some saints in the calendar; and all equally true. Even among modern divines, Bible Dictionary men, and such like, the most ridiculous tales concerning this bird continue to be propagated; and no small portion of them have been crowded into comments on this very verse. One specimen my old Psalter affords, which, for its curiosity, I shall lay before the reader: - <div eID="gen22029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22030" type="x-p"/> Trans. Newed sal be als of aeren thi youthed. <div eID="gen22030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22031" type="x-p"/> Par - The arne when he is greved with grete elde, his neb waxis so gretely, that he may nogt open his mouth and take mete: bot then he smytes his neb to the stane, and has away the solgh, and than he gaes til mete, and be commes yong a gayne. Swa Criste duse a way fra us oure elde of syn and mortalite, that settes us to ete oure brede in hevene, and newes us in hym. <div eID="gen22031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22032" type="x-p"/> The plain English of all this is: - "When the arne [eagle, from the Anglo-Saxon a word which Dr. Jamieson has not entered in his dictionary] is oppressed with old age, his bill grows so much that he cannot open his mouth in order to take meat. He then smites his bill against a stone, and breaks off the slough - the excrescence that prevented him from eating; and then he goes to his ordinary food, and becomes young again. So Christ takes away from us our old age of sin and death, and gives us to eat of that bread which comes down from heaven: and thus gives us a new life in himself." <div eID="gen22032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22033" type="x-p"/> I believe the meaning of the psalmist is much more simple: he refers to the moulting of birds, which, in most, takes place annually, in which they cast their old feathers and get a new plumage. To express this, he might as well have chosen any bird, as this is common to all the feathered race; but he chose the king of the birds, because of his bulk, his strength, and vivacity. <div eID="gen22033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22034" type="x-p"/> The long life of the eagle might have induced the psalmist to give it the preference. An eagle was nine years in the possession of Owen Holland, Esq., of Conway, in Wales, and had lived thirty-two years in the possession of the gentleman who made it a present to him: but of its previous age, for it came from Ireland, we are not informed. Keysler relates that an eagle died at Vienna, after a confinement of one hundred and four years! <div eID="gen22034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22035" type="x-p"/> The eagle can subsist a long time without food. That first mentioned above, through the neglect of a servant, was twenty-one days without food, and yet survived this long fast. <div eID="gen22035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22036" type="x-p"/> The meaning and moral of the psalmist are not difficult of comprehension. The Israelites, when redeemed from their captivity, should be so blessed by their God that they should reacquire their political strength and vigor; and should be so quickened by the Divine Spirit, that old things should be passed away, and all things become new.
entries.45e4b72f1a3e836c08978a159fb506527f8fda1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22037" type="x-p"/> The Lord executeth - This shall be done because the Lord will avenge his elect who have cried unto him day and night for his deliverance: "He is slow to anger;" but he will punish. "He is plenteous in mercy," and he will save. The persevering sinner shall be destroyed; the humble penitent shall be saved.
entries.45e676d319b997a1d1498d7368658345b029f1f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22038" type="x-p"/> He made known his ways unto Moses - From the earliest part of our history he has been our protector and defense. His wonderful acts in behalf of the children of Israel are so many proofs of his mercy, power, and goodness; and so many reasons why we should now trust in him.
entries.6a9d5ad092823ecafa6541df0210cbce0324fb0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22039" type="x-p"/> The Lord is merciful - See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.86.15">Psa 86:15</reference>.
entries.623f8705508ffac66dce953694d1ad0210f3ccc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22040" type="x-p"/> He will not always chide - He will not contend with us continually. He has often reproved, often punished us; but his mercy ever rejoiced over judgment.
entries.a808abd47d8db9a95606a6c90369d2764acaf6d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22041" type="x-p"/> He has not dealt with us after our sins - He has never apportioned our punishment to our sins, nor has he regulated the exercise of his mercy by our merits.
entries.1bafc961fcf0a82aceead91187baf085a6f6c71e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22042" type="x-p"/> For as the heaven is high above the earth - Great and provoking as our crimes may have been, yet his mercies have, in their magnitude and number, surpassed these, as far as the heavens are elevated beyond the earth.
entries.8ad9308705c8011e1e3f65a18b7ee0ea3f4f5ec7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22043" type="x-p"/> As far as the east is from the west - As the east and the west can never meet in one point, but be for ever at the same distance from each other, so our sins and their decreed punishment are removed to an eternal distance by his mercy.
entries.1eaa056b8512f7d64f7393473a79f1a2dfd0494f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22044" type="x-p"/> Like as a father pitieth his children - This is a very emphatic verse, and may be thus translated: "As the tender compassions of a father towards his children; so the tender compassicns of Jehovah towards them that fear him." Nothing can place the tenderness and concern of God for his creatures in a stronger light than this. What yearnings of bowels does a father feel toward the disobedient child, who, sensible of his ingratitude and disobedience, falls at his parent's feet, covered with confusion and melted into tears, with, "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am not worthy to be called thy son!" The same in kind, but infinitely more exquisite, does God feel when the penitent falls at his feet, and implores his mercy through Christ crucified.
entries.5c638bd11ca4ff424b5d4fed56cfeaddd4a0885c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen22044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22045" type="x-p"/> For he knoweth our frame - יצרנו yitsrenu, "our formation;" the manner in which we are constructed, and the materials of which we are made. He knows we cannot contend with him, and if he uses his power against us, we must be crushed to destruction. In all his conduct towards us he considers the frailty of our nature, the untowardness of our circumstances, the strength and subtlety of temptation, and the sure party (till the heart is renewed) that the tempter has within us. Though all these things are against us, yet it must ever be said, whatever use we make of it, "the grace of God is sufficient for us." But alas! alas! who makes use of that sufficient grace? Here, then, is cause for condemnation. But, O amazing mercy! if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him; for he knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are but dust. The man who can say, in the face of these Scriptures, Let us sin that grace may abound, is a brute and demon, who has neither lot nor part in this thing.
entries.887c25f6471ea8a9c8f46720d26cfeec4198388d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22046" type="x-p"/> His days are as grass - See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>.
entries.223accfd6d79a2f35e5361736f1979b7131aaca0: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22047" type="x-p"/> The wind passeth over it - Referring perhaps to some blasting pestilential wind.
entries.eef18320ca9167d7bec9610a61342d5cf69acac9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22048" type="x-p"/> The mercy of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting - חסד chesed signifies more particularly the exuberant goodness of God. This is an attribute of his nature, and must be from everlasting to everlasting; and hence, his righteousness (צדקת tsidketh) - his merciful mode of justifying the ungodly, is extended from one generation to another. <div eID="gen22048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22049" type="x-p"/> Unto children's children - It is still in force, and the doctrine of reconciliation through Christ shall continue to be preached till the conclusion of time.
entries.ab836ede6e2d047b9c2ea77a9747629dd0b6b114: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen22049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22050" type="x-p"/> To such as keep his convenant - The spirit of which was, I will be your God; We will be thy People. From the covenant came the commandments, and their obligation to remember and do them; and on such keepers of the covenant, and doers of the commandments, God promises to pour out his mercy through all generations.
entries.41bb2baa530a6cf44b11a56a5259418d15ae2a73: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22051" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath prepared his throne in the heavens - There he is Sovereign, but his dominion extends equally over all the earth; for his kingdom - regal government, influence, and sway, ruleth over all.
entries.2aa6079e379cd4e5ae3f7eaf1415b85dc28e1e8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22052" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord, ye his angels - Every person who has a sense of God's goodness to his soul feels his own powers inadequate to the praise which he ought to offer; and therefore naturally calls upon the holiest of men, and the supreme angels, to assist him in this work. <div eID="gen22052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22053" type="x-p"/> That excel in strength - Some take גברי כה gibborey coach the mighty in strength, for another class of the hierarchy, - they that do his commandments, hearkening to his words; and consider them to be that order of beings who are particularly employed in operations among and for the children of men; probably such as are called powers in the New Testament.
entries.e68af744c885995e69ab46d6f8d9209cb83960ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen22053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22054" type="x-p"/> All ye his hosts; ye ministers of his - We know almost nothing of the economy of the heavenly host; and, therefore, cannot tell what is the difference between angels, mighty powers, hosts, and ministers who do his pleasure. All owe their being and all its blessings to God; all depend upon his bounty; and without him they can do nothing; therefore, all should praise him.
entries.5ad3db1fdd225eb3bd9257d88cb8376f64eb6fca: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord, all his works - Let every thing he has done be so considered as to show forth his praise. <div eID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22056" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord, O my soul - Let me never forget my obligation to his mercy; for with tender mercies and loving-kindness has he crowned me. I will therefore be thankful unto him, and speak good of his name.  <chapter eID="Ps.103"/> <div eID="gen22056" type="x-p"/>

entries.3771c3b860225ce29648d9991b9a22485a070344: <div eID="gen9989" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hymn in Honour of God the All-Compassionate One</title> <div sID="gen9990" type="x-p"/> To the <hi type="italic">“Thou wilt have compassion upon Zion”</hi> of <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">Psa 102:14</reference> is appended Psalms 103, which has this as its substance throughout; but in other respects the two Psalms stand in contrast to one another. The inscription לדוד is also found thus by itself without any further addition even before Psalms of the First Book (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference>, Ps 35, Ps 37). It undoubtedly does not rest merely on conjecture, but upon tradition. For no internal grounds which might have given rise to the annotation לדוד can be traced. The form of the language does not favour it. This pensive song, so powerful in its tone, has an Aramaic colouring like Ps 116; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8">Psa 124:1-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1">Psa 129:1</reference>-8. In the heaping up of Aramaizing suffix-forms it has its equal only in the story of Elisha, 2Ki 4:1-7, where, moreover, the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> throughout substitutes the usual forms, whilst here, where these suffix-forms are intentional ornaments of the expression, the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> rightly remains unaltered. The forms are <hi type="italic">2nd sing. fem. ēchi</hi> for <hi type="italic">ēch</hi>, and <hi type="italic">2nd sing. plur.</hi> <hi type="italic">ājchi</hi> for <hi type="italic">ajich</hi>. The <hi type="italic">i</hi> without the tone which is added here is just the one with which originally the pronunciation was אתּי instead of אתּ and לכי for לך. Out of the Psalter (here and <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.19">Psa 116:19</reference>) these suffix-forms <hi type="italic">echi</hi> and <hi type="italic">ajchi</hi> occur only in <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jer 11:15</reference>, and in the North-Palestinian history of the prophet in the Book of Kings. The groups or strophes into which the Psalm falls are <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">Psa 103:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Psa 103:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.11">Psa 103:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.15">Psa 103:15</reference>, Psa 103:19. If we count their lines we obtain the schema 10. 10. 8. 8. 10. The coptic version accordingly reckons 46 <hi type="italic">CTYXOC</hi>, i.e., στίχοι.
entries.7485f7561a2a2b6fd2d1a0410e323c99cc3cf7b7: <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1-Ps.103.5">Psa 103:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen9990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9991" type="x-p"/> In the strophe <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">Psa 103:1</reference> the poet calls upon his soul to arise to praiseful gratitude for God’s justifying, redeeming, and renewing grace. In such soliloquies it is the Ego that speaks, gathering itself up with the spirit, the stronger, more manly part of man (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 104f.; tr. p. 126), or even, because the soul as the spiritual medium of the spirit and of the body represents the whole person of man (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 203; tr. p. 240), the Ego rendering objective in the soul the whole of its own personality. So here in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference> the soul, which is addressed, represents the whole man. The קובים which occurs here is a more choice expression for מעים (מעים): the heart, which is called קרב κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν, the reins, the liver, etc.; for according to the scriptural conception (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 266; tr. p. 313) these organs of the cavities of the breast and abdomen serve not merely for the bodily life, but also the psycho-spiritual life. The summoning בּרכי is repeated <hi type="italic">per anaphoram</hi>. There is nothing the soul of man is so prone to forget as to render thanks that are due, and more especially thanks that are due to God. It therefore needs to be expressly aroused in order that it may not leave the blessing with which God blesses it unacknowledged, and may not forget all His acts performed (גּמל = גּמר) on it (גּמוּל, ῥῆμα μέσον, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>), which are purely deeds of loving-kindness), which is the primal condition and the foundation of all the others, viz., sin-pardoning mercy. The verbs סלח and רפא with a dative of the object denote the bestowment of that which is expressed by the verbal notion. תּחלוּאים (taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.29.21">Deu 29:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.19">1Ch 21:19</reference>, from חלא = חלה, root הל, <hi type="italic">solutum, laxum esse</hi>) are not merely bodily diseases, but all kinds of inward and outward sufferings. משּׁחת the lxx renders ἐκ φθορᾶς (from שׁחת, as in <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job 17:14</reference>); but in this antithesis to life it is more natural to render the “pit” (from שׁוּח) as a name of Hades, as in Psa 16:10. Just as the soul owes its deliverance from guilt and distress and death to God, so also does it owe to God that with which it is endowed out of the riches of divine love. The verb עטּר, without any such addition as in Ps 5:13, is “to crown,” cf. Psa 8:6. As is usually the case, it is construed with a double accusative; the crown is as it were woven out of loving-kindness and compassion. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּטּוב in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference> instead of the accusative (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.28">Psa 104:28</reference>) denotes the means of satisfaction, which is at the same time that which satisfies. עדיך the Targum renders: <hi type="italic">dies senectutis tuae</hi>, whereas in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference> it is <hi type="italic">ornatus ejus</hi>; the Peshîto renders: <hi type="italic">corpus tuum</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference> inversely, <hi type="italic">juventus eorum</hi>. These significations, “old age” or “youth,” are pure inventions. And since the words are addressed to the soul, עדי cannot also, like כבוד in other instances, be a name of the soul itself (Aben-Ezra, Mendelssohn, Philippsohn, Hengstenberg, and others). We, therefore, with Hitzig, fall back upon the sense of the word in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>, where the lxx renders τάς σιαγόνας αὐτῶν, but here more freely, apparently starting from the primary notion of עדי = Arabic <hi type="italic">chadd</hi>, the cheek: τὸν ἐμπιπλῶντα ἐν ἀγαθοῖς τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν σου (whereas Saadia’s <hi type="italic">victum tuum</hi> is based upon a comparison of the Arabic <hi type="italic">gdâ</hi>, to nourish). The poet tells the soul (i.e., his own person, himself) that God satisfies it with good, so that it as it were gets its cheeks full of it (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11">Psa 81:11</reference>). The comparison כּנּשׁר is, as in Mic 1:16 (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>), to be referred to the annual moulting of the eagle. Its renewing of its plumage is an emblem of the renovation of his youth by grace. The predicate to נעוּריכי (plural of extension in relation to time) stands first regularly in the <hi type="italic">sing. fem</hi>.
entries.7cff25582a85fa715d1256056b6c523f84c609d3: <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6-Ps.103.10">Psa 103:6-10</reference> <div eID="gen9991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9992" type="x-p"/> His range of vision being widened from himself, the poet now in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Psa 103:6</reference> describes God’s gracious and fatherly conduct towards sinful and perishing men, and that as it shines forth from the history of Israel and is known and recognised in the light of revelation. What <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Psa 103:6</reference> says is a common-place drawn from the history of Israel. משׁפּטים is an accusative governed by the עשׂה that is to be borrowed out of עשׂה (so Baer after the Masora). And because <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Psa 103:6</reference> is the result of an historical retrospect and survey, יודיע in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.7">Psa 103:7</reference> can affirm that which happened in the past (cf. Psa 96:6.); for the supposition of Hengstenberg and Hitzig, that <hi type="italic">Moses</hi> here represents Israel like <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi>, <hi type="italic">Isaac</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi> in other instances, is without example in the whole Israelitish literature. It becomes clear from <reference osisRef="Ps.103.8">Psa 103:8</reference> in what sense the making of His ways known is meant. The poet has in his mind Moses’ prayer: “make known to me now Thy way” (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.13">Exo 33:13</reference>), which Jahve fulfilled by passing by him as he stood in the cleft of the rock and making Himself visible to him as he looked after Him, amidst the proclamation of His attributes. The ways of Jahve are therefore in this passage not those in which men are to walk in accordance with His precepts (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference>), but those which He Himself follows in the course of His redemptive history (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.3">Psa 67:3</reference>). The confession drawn from Exo 34:6. is become a formula of the Israelitish faith (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">Psa 86:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.8">Psa 145:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joe 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.17">Neh 9:17</reference>, and frequently). In Psa 103:9. the fourth attribute (ורב־חסד) is made the object of further praise. He is not only long (ארך from ארך, like כּבד from כּבד) in anger, i.e., waiting a long time before He lets His anger loose, but when He contends, i.e., interposes judicially, this too is not carried to the full extent (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>), He is not angry for ever (נטר, to keep, viz., anger, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Amo 1:11</reference>; cf. the parallels, both as to matter and words, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jer 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.16">Isa 57:16</reference>). The procedure of His righteousness is regulated not according to our sins, but according to His purpose of mercy. The prefects in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.10">Psa 103:10</reference> state that which God has constantly not done, and the futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference> what He continually will not do.
entries.d49efa6e0475befd134d32b03f8c036e8b20a2fa: <reference osisRef="Ps.103.11-Ps.103.14">Psa 103:11-14</reference> <div eID="gen9992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9993" type="x-p"/> The ingenious figures in Psa 103:11. (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.11">Psa 57:11</reference>) illustrate the infinite power and complete unreservedness of mercy (loving-kindness). הרחיק has <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> (as have also השׁחיתו and התעיבו, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.53.2">Psa 53:2</reference>, in exact texts), in order to render possible the distinct pronunciation of the guttural in the combination רח. <reference osisRef="Ps.103.13">Psa 103:13</reference> sounds just as much like the spirit of the New Testament as <reference osisRef="Ps.103.11">Psa 103:11</reference>, Psa 103:12. The relationship to Jahve in which those stand who fear Him is a filial relationship based upon free reciprocity (Mal 3:11). His Fatherly compassion is (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>) based upon the frailty and perishableness of man, which are known to God, much the same as God’s promise after the Flood not to decree a like judgment again (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen 8:21</reference>). According to this passage and <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>, יצרנוּ appears to be intended of the moral nature; but according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference></hi>, one is obliged to think rather of the natural form which man possesses from God the Creator (ויּיצר, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>) than of the form of heart which he has by his own choice and, so far as its groundwork is concerned, by inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.7">Psa 51:7</reference>). In זכוּר, mindful, the passive, according to Böttcher’s correct apprehension of it, expresses a passive state after an action that is completed by the person himself, as in בּטוּה, ידוּע, and the like. In its form <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference></hi> reminds one of the Book of Job <reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.23">Job 28:23</reference>, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference></hi> as to subject-matter recalls <reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference>, and other passages (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.39">Psa 78:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.48">Psa 89:48</reference>); but the following figurative representation of human frailty, with which the poet contrasts the eternal nature of the divine mercy as the sure stay of all God-fearing ones in the midst of the rise and decay of things here below, still more strongly recalls that book.
entries.19445992a2478b65aaea1660712b1f48879aff85: <reference osisRef="Ps.103.15-Ps.103.18">Psa 103:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen9993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9994" type="x-p"/> The figure of the grass recalls Psa 90:5., cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Isa 40:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference>; that of the flower, Job 14:2. אנושׁ is man as a mortal being; his life’s duration is likened to that of a blade of grass, and his beauty and glory to a flower of the field, whose fullest bloom is also the beginning of its fading. In <reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference> בּו (the same as in Isa 40:7.) refers to man, who is compared to grass and flowers. כּי is ἐάν with a hypothetical perfect; and the wind that scorches up the plants, referred to man, is an emblem of every form of peril that threatens life: often enough it is really a breath of wind which snaps off a man’s life. The bold designation of vanishing away without leaving any trace, “and his place knoweth him no more,” is taken from <reference osisRef="Job.7.10">Job 7:10</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">ibid</hi>. <reference osisRef="Job.8.18">Job 8:18</reference>; Job 20:9. In the midst of this plant-like, frail destiny, there is, however, one strong ground of comfort. There is an everlasting power, which raises all those who link themselves with it above the transitoriness involved in nature’s laws, and makes them eternal like itself. This power is the mercy of God, which spans itself above (על) all those who fear Him like an eternal heaven. This is God’s righteousness, which rewards faithful adherence to His covenant and conscientious fulfilment of His precepts in accordance with the order of redemption, and shows itself even to (ל) children’s children, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.20.6">Exo 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.9">Deu 7:9</reference> : on into a thousand generations, i.e., into infinity.
entries.8aec9f72e8c2281a7f9c09c018f93c5bbf081aa1: <reference osisRef="Ps.103.19-Ps.103.22">Psa 103:19-22</reference> <div eID="gen9994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9995" type="x-p"/> He is able to show Himself thus gracious to His own, for He is the supra-mundane, all-ruling King. With this thought the poet draws on to the close of his song of praise. The heavens in opposition to the earth, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Ecc 5:12</reference>, is the unchangeable realm above the rise and fall of things here below. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Psa 103:19</reference></hi> cf. 1Ch 29:12. בּכּל refers to everything created without exception, the universe of created things. In connection with the heavens of glory the poet cannot but call to mind the angels. His call to these to join in the praise of Jahve has its parallel only in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.148.1">Psa 148:1</reference>-14. It arises from the consciousness of the church on earth that it stands in living like-minded fellowship with the angels of God, and that it possesses a dignity which rises above all created things, even the angels which are appointed to serve it (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">Psa 91:11</reference>). They are called גּבּרים as in <reference osisRef="Joel.3.11">Joe 3:11</reference>, and in fact גּבּרי כּח, as the strong to whom belongs strength unequalled. Their life endowed with heroic strength is spent entirely - an example for mortals - in an obedient execution of the word of God. לשׁמע is a definition not of the purpose, but of the manner: <hi type="italic">obediendo</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen 2:3</reference> <hi type="italic">perficiendo</hi>). Hearing the call of His word, they also forthwith put it into execution. the hosts (צבאיו), as משׁרתיו shows, are the celestial spirits gathered around the angels of a higher rank (cf. <reference osisRef="Luke.2.13">Luk 2:13</reference>), the innumerable λειτουργικὰ πνεῦματα (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">Psa 104:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Dan 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">Heb 1:14</reference>), for there is a <hi type="italic">hierarchia caelestis</hi>. From the archangels the poet comes to the myriads of the heavenly hosts, and from these to all creatures, that they, wheresoever they may be throughout Jahve’s wide domain, may join in the song of praise that is to be struck up; and from this point he comes back to his own soul, which he modestly includes among the creatures mentioned in the third passage. A threefold בּרכי נפשׁי now corresponds to the threefold בּרכוּ; and inasmuch as the poet thus comes back to his own soul, his Psalm also turns back into itself and assumes the form of a converging circle.  <chapter eID="Ps.103"/> <div eID="gen9995" type="x-p"/>

entries.e629c5557cebbc55a83f6b92874cf4523456de6c:
PSALM 103
By this psalm every godly man is taught to give thanks to God for the mercies bestowed upon himself in particular, and then for the grace which God has vouchsafed to all his chosen ones in common, by making a covenant of salvation with them in his law, that he might make them partakers of his adoption. But the Psalmist chiefly magnifies the mercy by which God sustains and bears with his people; and that not on account of any merit or worth of theirs, for they only deserve to be visited with severe punishment, but because he compassionates their frailty. The psalm is at length concluded with a general ascription of praise to God.
Psalm 103:1-5
A Psalm of David.
The author of this beautiful and affecting psalm was David; but the time and occasion of its composition are uncertain. Some are of opinion that it is a song of gratitude for David’s recovery from some dangerous sickness. Others think it was written upon his receiving assurance that his great sin in the case of Bathsheba and Uriah was forgiven. “I am not prepared to say,” observes Walford, “that this judgment is certainly correct; but as it is a subject of no great moment, am willing to acquiesce in it. If it be correct, then we have two of the most instructive examples of enlightened and fervent piety, which are contained in the Holy Scriptures, occasioned by one failure in the conduct of a good man, who was habitually remarkable for his steadfast obedience to the laws of God. The one of these examples is in Psalm 51, in which the sacred writer records his deep and humble penitence: and the other, which is now before us, displays the feelings of sacred joy and thankfulness, in terms that are most delightful and consolatory. So admirably adapted are these two psalms to the varied sentiments and emotions of Christian feeling, that I can scarcely suppose any real believer of the gospel is to be found who has not, on multiplied occasions, made them the objects of his attentive meditation, so as to have, if not the express words, yet the sense of them, engraven on his heart and memory, in characters never to be effaced but by death.”
1. Bless Jehovah, O my soul! and all my inward parts, bless his holy name. 2. Bless Jehovah, O my soul! and forget not any of his benefits: 3. Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases; 4. Who redeemeth thy life from the grave; who crowneth
“Ou, envirrone.” — Fr. marg. “Or, surroundeth.”
thee with mercy and compassions; 5. Who satisfieth [or filleth] thy mouth with good: thy youth shall be renewed as the eagle’s.
Walford’s rendering of this verse is as follows: —
“Who satisfieth thy advancing age with good; Thy youth is renewed as the eagle’s.”
In defense of reading “thy advancing age” instead of “thy mouth” as it is in our English translation, and as Calvin has it, he observes, “The version here adopted is that of the Chaldee, and is supported by the parallelism in the following clause.”
 
1. Bless Jehovah, O my soul! The prophet, by stirring up himself to gratitude, gives by his own example a lesson to every man of the duty incumbent upon him. And doubtless our slothfulness in this matter has need of continual incitement. If even the prophet, who was inflamed with a more intense and fervent zeal than other men, was not free from this malady, of which his earnestness in stimulating himself is a plain confession, how much more necessary is it for us, who have abundant experience of our own torpor, to apply the same means for our quickening? The Holy Spirit, by his mouth, indirectly upbraids us on account of our not being more diligent in praising God, and at the same time points out the remedy, that every man may descend into himself and correct his own sluggishness. Not content with calling upon his soul (by which he unquestionably means the seat of the understanding and affections) to bless God, the prophet expressly adds his inward parts, addressing as it were his own mind and heart, and all the faculties of both. When he thus speaks to himself, it is as if, removed from the presence of men, he examined himself before God. The repetition renders his language still more emphatic, as if he thereby intended to reprove his own slothfulness.
